summary: Intro discovery for Private (VPC) deployment. Customer runs critical workloads in AWS across us-east-1 and eu-west-1, wants private endpoints, no public internet egress for data plane, strict KMS controls, and pilot to validate latency/cost. Redwood AE/SE to share network checklist and security docs and schedule technical deep dive.
transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-05-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Rivera (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (CTO - Sylvan), Maya Singh (Cloud Architect), Ethan Lowe (Security Lead), Priya Nair (SRE)

Agenda: 1) Quick intros 2) Current infra + constraints 3) Networking requirements (peering, private endpoints) 4) Security/compliance (KMS, audit) 5) Pilot next steps

[00:00] Alyssa: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm alyssa with redwood, this is marco our se, want to run through your private vpc needs and see if dedicated or private makes sense
[00:18] Daniel: yeah thanks, we'll keep it tight. I'm daniel, cto. sylvan runs most of our infra in aws, us-east-1 primary, eu-west-1 for eu customers. main ask is we need private-only connectivity for the inference plane — no public internet egress for model requests or logs.
[00:36] Marco: great, do you have an existing peering pattern across accounts? are you using transit gateway or direct peering?
[00:44] Maya: we use a transit gateway in us-east-1, but we have multiple accounts behind it. for eu we have a separate transit gateway in eu-west. prefer transit gateway peering but open to PrivateLink if easier.
[01:10] Alyssa: ok got it, so two options typically: VPC peering/transit-gw for full routing or PrivateLink/Interface endpoints for more explicit flows. for our private option we can either place redwood nodes in your VPC or provide private endpoints — depends on your security posture.
[01:33] Ethan: quick question: if you place nodes in our VPC, how do you handle key management? we need KMS control and bring-your-own-key support, plus audit logs going to our account.
[01:46] Marco: we support customer-managed KMS and can integrate with your KMS via cross-account grants. audit logs can be routed to your cloudwatch or s3 in your account. there's an HSM option for higher assurance but that's based on dedicated private deployments.
[02:08] Priya: when you say "nodes in our VPC" do you mean full VMs with ENIs or some managed endpoint we talk to?
[02:15] Marco: typically we run inference instances as managed instances in a customer-controlled VPC via an agent; they show up as ENIs in your account. requests never traverse the public internet. alternative is PrivateLink where you call an endpoint and traffic stays within aws backbone but route tables are simpler.
[02:39] Daniel: latency is critical for some usecases — we have a trading-ish near-real-time pipeline, so sub-100ms p95 is preferred. cost matters too, so we might prefer shared/dedicated vs fully private nodes depending on price delta.
[02:58] Alyssa: totally. for latency you can pin to region and we can provision local capacity. dedicated reserved pools give predictable throughput and lower p95 than hosted with region fallback. private/on-prem options trade off cost for isolation.
[03:18] Maya: can you support cross-region access? our app is in us-east but some data lives in eu-west, and we may need models close to both.
[03:28] Marco: yes we can deploy in multiple regions; the control plane can be in redwood's hosted control plane or private control plane depending on the deal. if you require full private control plane in your network, that adds extra ops but we have a VPC-only control plane option.
[03:45] Ethan: about egress — we can't allow outbound to internet for model artifacts or telemetry. any egress for updates, patching?
[03:55] Marco: patching is handled via your private patch endpoints or via scheduled pull from internal sources. we support air-gapped or restricted egress patterns; we'll need to map which IPs and ports to allow for occasional control connectivity if you choose hosted control plane.
[04:16] Maya: what about DNS and routing? we use split-horizon DNS and have strict IAM.
[04:23] Marco: we can support private DNS zones; ENIs can register internal hostnames. routing can be via TGW attachments or peering; we'll share the network checklist with exact CIDRs, ports (gRPC/HTTPS), and DNS recommendations.
[04:41] Alyssa: are there any compliance must-haves beyond SOC 2 — e.g., data residency, regulatory audits?
[04:48] Daniel: we need EU data residency for customer PII, and SOC2 plus some industry audits. also SAML for SSO and RBAC integration with our idp.
[04:58] Marco: we support SAML/SSO and can integrate with your idp. RBAC can map to your groups. for data residency we recommend hosting inference in the same region as the data; we can restrict model deployments to specific regions via policy.
[05:20] Priya: any limitations on model sizes or quantized formats? we plan to run a mix of open models and some custom fine-tuned models.
[05:29] Marco: we support a wide catalog and custom models; runtime constraints depend on GPU/instance type. for private deployments we can select GPU types and also provide quantization recommendations. we'll need model size and throughput estimates for the pilot.
[05:46] Daniel: okay, practical ask: show us how peering would look. we prefer TGW peering if possible — less routing complexity.
[05:55] Alyssa: noted. we'll send a TGW peering diagram and a PrivateLink option too. also include required IAM roles and cross-account grant templates.
[06:06] Maya: what about private endpoints — do you expose per-service endpoints or a single ingress? we like having an interface endpoint that our services can call internally.
[06:15] Marco: you can have multiple interface endpoints per region for different routes (generation, embeddings). we typically recommend separate endpoints for telemetry and inference to control egress and apply different security policies.
[06:33] Ethan: encryption at rest and in transit — do you manage certs or we do?
[06:38] Marco: TLS in transit with mTLS option if you want mutual TLS. for at-rest we can integrate with your KMS. cert management can be via your PKI or our managed certs depending on control plane configuration.
[06:57] Daniel: any public IPs required on the inference nodes? we don't allow public IPs in our prod VPCs.
[07:03] Marco: no, we do not require public IPs; ENIs in private subnets are fine. for outbound control traffic we can put a NAT in a management VPC or use VPC endpoints depending on your architecture.
[07:19] Priya: curious about monitoring and logs — where do the logs go and can we keep logs within our account?
[07:26] Marco: logs/metrics can be forwarded to your CloudWatch or an S3 bucket in your account. we can also mirror trace spans to your tracing system. we provide token-level cost and latency breakdowns but you can choose retention policies.
[07:44] Alyssa: sounds good. let's talk pilot scope — what would you want to validate in a two-week pilot?
[07:50] Daniel: baseline latency p50/p95 for our 256-token prompts, throughput for peak 100 rps, and security posture — KMS integration and private connectivity.
[08:02] Marco: perfect. we'll ask for a sample of your prompt distribution and expected concurrency. we'll propose a pilot with a small dedicated pool in us-east-1 and one in eu-west-1 if needed, or a single-region pilot to start.
[08:18] Maya: cost: can you give rough delta between shared hosted vs private nodes? our finance will want ballpark numbers before committing to ops work.
[08:26] Alyssa: we'll include a preliminary cost model in the follow-up: hosted api vs dedicated reserved vs private VPC pricing, plus expected token/unit costs.
[08:36] Ethan: any known blockers for us connecting from an on-prem environment into the VPC? we have a datacenter that peered with aws via direct connect.
[08:45] Marco: Direct Connect plus TGW is supported; we can route through your existing direct connect to reach the inference nodes in the VPC. we'll need to validate route propagation and BGP.
[09:00] Daniel: what's the timeline to get a private deployment up for pilot?
[09:05] Alyssa: typical pilot turnaround 2-4 weeks once we have network details and model artifacts; dedicated/private deployments skew toward the longer end. initial demo/pilot could be 2 weeks if we keep scope tight.
[09:17] Maya: any special firewall ports? we prefer granular lists so security can sign off.
[09:23] Marco: yes, we'll include ports (443 gRPC over TLS, management ports for agent heartbeat), and exact CIDRs. list will be in checklist.
[09:37] Priya: are there any managed connectors for secret storage? we use AWS Secrets Manager and HashiCorp Vault in some apps.
[09:45] Marco: we can integrate with Secrets Manager natively; Vault can be integrated via sidecars/agent. for KMS we prefer cross-account grants to avoid moving keys.
[09:58] Daniel: another thing — we need to ensure no model weights or cached KV data persists outside our control. how do you handle caching and kv cache in private deployments?
[10:09] Marco: KV "cash" — i mean KV cache — lives on instance local SSDs and is scoped per tenant; for private deployments we can configure cache eviction and ensure snapshots aren't written to external object stores unless you opt in. logs and metrics are exported under your account.
[10:29] Alyssa: quick check — you mentioned air-gapped possibility earlier?
[10:33] Ethan: yes, low egress.
[10:35] Marco: for air-gapped we can deliver an on-prem package, but that requires longer lead time and manual patching. most customers choose private VPC with restricted egress.
[10:47] Maya: okay, sounds reasonable. can you also show us the control plane differences? we prefer a minimal hosted control plane that only manages metadata vs a private control plane with no outside visibility.
[10:58] Marco: sure. hosted control plane means management plane is in redwood's cloud; control messages may cross public endpoints but we can restrict by IP allowlist and VPN. private control plane runs in your VPC or a dedicated account; it provides full control but increases ops surface. we'll include pros/cons in the follow-up doc.
[11:20] Daniel: team-members — who should we involve for the deep dive? networking, security, and a platform engineer; i'll loop them in.
[11:27] Alyssa: perfect. Marco, anything else technical to call out?
[11:31] Marco: just that for benchmarking we'll need sample request traces, token sizes, concurrency targets, and model list (sizes + whether quantized). we'll also ask for a preferred region for pilot and any cust-managed image requirements.
[11:48] Priya: can you run inference on spot instances for cost savings or do you recommend reserved?
[11:54] Marco: we can run mixed pools; for critical low-latency workloads we recommend reserved/dedicated GPU pools. batchy or non-critical jobs can use spot-backed nodes. we'll note recommendations.
[12:06] Daniel: any gotchas with AWS account limits or ENI quotas?
[12:10] Marco: possibly, large deployments can hit ENI or EIP quotas; we'll include guidance on requesting quota increases and typical counts per instance size.
[12:22] Alyssa: recap and next steps — we'll send network checklist, TGW peering diagram, SOC2/security doc, and a draft pilot proposal with cost estimates. we'll also schedule the technical deep dive next week.
[12:39] Daniel: sounds good. thanks for the clear action items.
[12:44] Priya: thanks all.
[12:47] Alyssa: thanks everyone, i'll send the follow-up by friday.

(Transcript contains occasional transcription errors: e.g., "KV cash" instead of KV cache, speaker attribution may be approximate.)
